summary.title: A dirty dozen: twelve common metric interpretation pitfalls in online controlled experiments
summary.one_liner: Twelve ways misreading A/B test metrics leads to wrong ship decisions, with Microsoft examples and the checks that guard against each one.
keywords: what is a sample ratio mismatch
why did my a/b test metric go down
takeaways: Check data quality first: a treatment-to-control user ratio mismatch means the metric values cannot be trusted.
Define count metrics for numerators and denominators of ratio metrics so denominator shifts are visible.
Run a power analysis before the experiment, aiming for at least 80% power on OEC and guardrail metrics, and do not treat non-significant results as no change.
Do not stop experiments early or extend them for significance; re-run borderline results and watch for novelty or primacy effects.
Treat surprising metric moves with skepticism (Twyman's law) and segment results over time and by group, watching for Simpson's paradox.
summary.summary: This blog post by Adrian Colyer summarises a KDD 2017 paper by Dmitriev et al. from Microsoft, which lists twelve common mistakes when interpreting metrics in A/B tests. It begins with the four metric classes Microsoft uses: data quality, overall evaluation criteria (OEC), guardrail, and local feature/diagnostic metrics. Each pitfall is then illustrated with a real experiment from MSN, Bing or Skype, such as a sample ratio mismatch that inflated page load time and a telemetry loss bias from push notifications. For each pitfall the post gives the recommended detection or prevention step, such as automated mismatch alerts, re-running borderline p-values, or funnel metrics using conditional and unconditional rates.
